utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could the witness be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Please be seated, Mr. Mrksic. Mr. Mrksic, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The same position as last week, Your Honour. We don't have any questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Mikulicic, and Mr. Mikulicic is counsel for Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Mrksic. On behalf of the Defence for General Markac, I will put several questions to you, and I kindly ask you to answer them to the best of your recollection. At the same time, I do ask you to give your answers slowly so that the interpreters can do their job properly, and that we do not get questions and answers confused. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Perhaps I will be better at it today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, sometime in mid-May, 1995, or, to be precise, on the 18th, you took up the position of the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, briefly, what the structure of the Main Staff was, in terms of how it was organised?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff, just as all the structures of that level, had its operational organ, which was the Chief of Staff, then the rear logistics organ, security organ, organ for moral guidance, and personnel organ, which were attached to the Chief of Staff. That would be the basic structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You also had your assistants in the Main Staff. How many were there, and which duties were they charged with?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the Chief of Staff until the start of war. As soon as the war breaks out, I take up that position, and the position of the supreme commander is taken by Mile Martic. I had my assistant for logistics, assistant for moral guidance - he was Kosta Novakovic - the assistant for security, whose name I can't recall, and the -- or rather the security and intelligence assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In other words, you had the security assistant, you also had the security department?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was Colonel Rade Raseta your security officer?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They rotated frequently. I didn't know him from before. I didn't know what his background was. I think that he held that position only briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That was to be my next question. Did you appoint him there or did you find him there in the staff? But you've just answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found all of them when I came there, holding these positions, save for the commanders of the Special Units Corps. They had already been holding these positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was your relationship with the assistants of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our relations were always official. I didn't have any problems, and my authority was of the kind that it never would happen that I would come up against obedience on the part of my subordinates, and I always maintained discipline. That's what the staff was. I always appreciated whenever my associates were quite open and candid in their views in one-on-one conversations. I had very good relations with Bjelanovic, with Bjelanovic, who was a very experienced officer - he was a general - who had been there for quite a long time. He knew the people and their mindset.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, during your testimony you said that you were confronted with a situation that you tried to struggle with, and that was the issue of the so-called Daddy's sons who engaged in black-marketeering?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As the commander of the Main Staff of the ARSK, how did you approach the situation and combat these actions?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't want to proceed to take any course of action before a decision was taken by those who had dispatched me there and by the top leadership of the RSK, as well as the structures of Western Bosnia and all others involved, until such time as the border with Western Bosnia is closed. I could not create conditions for peace and peaceful integration as long as black-marketeering and smuggling was going on in my area. I placed this as a demand on my subordinates, and they all obeyed me, in terms of applying various measures. As for these Daddy's boys, even if non -- even if all the other structures felt that they were the untouchables, I, with my Special Units Corps, did enforce law and order. Thus, UNPROFOR's vehicles were no longer seized, commanders were not faced with threats, and they felt this change of atmosphere, which was beneficial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was the role of the Security Department in this particular activity aimed at combatting marketeering; did they have a role to play in this?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security organs did have information as to who committed these actions. This was a matter for the Security Department as well as Intelligence Department. On all the warring parties, the situation was the same. They would always involve these officers in order to obtain information about black-marketeering that was going on on all sides. Everybody was both sellers and buyers. When I asked for the information to be collected, they told me that since I had forbidden them to be in contact with these individuals, it was difficult to obtain information. I don't know if you understand me. And this was not the case isolated to the RSK, it was widespread, and this is how some of the individuals managed to earn their first couple of million.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was waiting for you to finish your -- for the interpretation to finish. Did there come to appear in your work the situation that the Security Department collected accurate information about the incidents of marketeering taking place in your area?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think the matters were completely truthful. I think that there were different interests at play there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us move on to a different topic, Mr. Mrksic. In your earlier testimony, you portrayed for us the strategic situation in the area under your command. My next couple of questions will focus on the area of Velebit and Gracac. You explained to us what the strategic importance of Gracac was, and if my understanding is correct, and you'll correct me if I'm wrong, its importance lay in particular with relation to the Gospic-Luka-Gracac road and on to Otric and Srb, in order to prevent the ARSK forces from ending up in an encirclement. Since you were informed in advance of the commencement of Operation Storm, what was the axis along which you expected the Croatian forces to launch their attack in that particular region?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attack did transpire according to our expectations, but there was fighting around Zubovi, up around the repeater up on Velebit. We tried to enforce our positions there. The brigade commander received assignments to that effect. However, what happened was that the peak of Velebit was captured, which made the whole defence along Gospic toward Gracac very vulnerable. When the repeater was destroyed -- partly destroyed and then also captured, we lost all communication with the rest of RSK and with Belgrade. According to the information I had, it was the Special Police that headed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The advancement from the peak of Velebit towards the Gospic-Gracac road, which sits in the valley, was it of strategic importance, in terms of the conduct of defence?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was important for the Lika Corps because there was the danger that -- or, rather, there were -- there were problems with the Dalmatia Corps, the events you mentioned around Gospic. The special units, which were trained for such difficult terrain, had an ally in the local population there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The area was defended by the Gracac Brigade, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Gracac Brigade that defended the area up there, and there was the Zub feature, which is on an elevation of 1.800 metres. I think it was held by the Obrovac Brigade. That's where the boundary between the two brigade AORs was, and that's where the breakthrough occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If you'll recall today, where was it that you planned the second line of defence was to be?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Lika Corps had a very shallow area, and the plan was to hold that first line of defence that had been in preparation for four years. We didn't plan for any fall-back positions. I deployed some other brigades, and I forgot what the name of the place along that axis was, in order to close the ranks so that they wouldn't be able to break through towards Otric. Our -- that was the gist of our concept, because this was the area of 15 to 20 kilometres depth, at most. That's the sort of an area where you would be able to deploy a brigade. One can only create an operational depth where you have a strip of land that is larger than 20 kilometres, which we didn't have. That's why we expected frontal combat would take place and not to be attacked from the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You explained to us what the significance of the Celavac repeater was?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you recall when it was that communications were severed once the Celavac repeater was captured?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in the afternoon at around 1.00 p.m. that I received first reports from corps commanders and talked to them over the radio. Subsequently, all the lines were down and I could not -- no longer be in contact with them. All the subsequent communication we had were down, in fact, as in World War II. That's what I remember. Whether it was at 1.00 or 2.00, but I do know that in early afternoon I received combat reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When did the 9th Gracac Brigade retreat from that area of Krajina and along which axis?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you the details. It should be for the corps commander to know the information. I was aware of where the main lines of deployment of corps were. I didn't have information for specific brigades. I know that the first brigade to encounter problems was the Lika Brigade, defending the area opposite Ogulin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Will this jog your memory if I tell you that the Gracac Brigade withdrew across Gracac, via Otric, and on towards Srb? Is this consistent with how you remember these events?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say so. I don't remember this specifically. If you have this piece of information, there's no reason I should doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In an earlier testimony, and I'm referring to D1514 and D923, we were able to see that the Main Staff was relocated from Knin to Srb sometime after midnight on the 5th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the elements that were relocated were relocated before the start of the aggression. This was part of a plan, that there had to be a reserve -- alternate command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Similarly, you told us with the commencement of the Operation Storm, there were very few members of the RSK government in Knin, that most of them were outside of the Krajina borders?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can name them; perhaps not all of them. There was the minister of interior, minister of defence, who were in Knin. There was the official charged with social welfare, minister of social welfare, Strbac. He was a young man. Then there was the president of the assembly who was there, the president of the republic, along with his organs. It was the prime minister and minister of foreign affairs who left for Belgrade. There was also the finance minister, who was in Knin. Later on, I learned that he had taken the money from the SDK. It was a strong team that remained there, and some of them left for Belgrade on orders in order to see what could be salvaged and how war could be averted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, under the circumstances where the Main Staff was relocated to Srb, and subsequently or at the same time, the government was relocated, certain members of the government were not present in Krajina. The communications, due to the fall of the Celavac repeater, were down. Under these circumstances, how did the political and military authorities operate? And I'm referring to the 5th and 6th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me explain this to you now. Before the start of the aggression, together with the president and the top leadership, I made an assessment of the possibility that this should happen; we would lose all communication if we have forces on the Adriatic Sea that could interfere with the communications. And I knew that the repeat could be captured, so I asked for a scenario to be developed as to how we could function without the communications. On the 4th, I sent a helicopter, once the Supreme Defence Council met. The minister president allowed for minister of the interior, Toso Paic, to go to the areas of Kordun as a representative of the government. Mile Novakovic, who had just come back from negotiations, he was a general, the commander charged with political issues, and he was prepared to engage in negotiations with the Croatian government on my behalf because he would be an individual who would more appropriately be the negotiator. He was charged with coordinating the special corps, the Banija and Kordun Corps, as well as -- so coordinating these forces with Fikret Abdic's forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I apologise if I interrupt you. We've steered away from the topic.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just told you who the members of the government were who were present in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: General Mrksic, could I ask you to make a break between question and answer, and could I ask you the same, Mr. Mikulicic, because it's impossible to follow for the interpreters at this speed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could also the witness speak away from the microphones, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, you are requested to take a bit of distance to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What I'm primarily interested in is: In these difficult circumstances, how did the functioning of the command and the political leadership function on the 5th and the 6th of August, when the communications were interrupted, when regular institutions of the staff and the government seat were relocated? What were the difficulties there?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The difficulties were that there was no direct contact. My voice was not being heard. Flyers were being thrown around. Nobody was being able to hear me over the media, and I had new information. It was difficult to believe what they were being served. It was a very difficult situation, sir, very difficult. I said that they had been missing their mothers, they were crying. But this doesn't refer only to me; it was a general situation. We were thrown into the clutches of all the most modern systems of propaganda, ranging from a television that appeared with a new name -- actually, with the same name as the one from before, except the person behind the camera was not the one from before, but a new one, but it functioned the way it functioned. It was very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In such a situation, there was a division between the Army of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina to the southern and northern sections?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As briefly as possible, can you explain, how did this division occur and what were the consequences of such a division of the army?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the consequences arose from the attack on Knin from the Grahovac direction, with the fall of Grahovac, all the problems came from there. But the Kordun-Banija Corps and partially the Lika Corps were putting up resistance for as long as they were able to, until they came to the position to fight in the environment. Then the Banija Corps sustained a lot of losses. The Kordun Corps was not even touched, nobody was attacking. They were objecting to having to withdraw at all. And that is how it occurred that we always planned, and we always were in this danger that our Krajina would be divided into two zones, north and south, from Ogulin, with the valley -- valley through the Vlasko [phoen], towards Bihac, and that's why all these combinations of ours around Pauk and all of these forces around holding this area, creating the corps, the special units, were served -- were aimed at preventing this division from occurring.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But it did take place, in any case, did it not?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: My next question: After the Main Staff was relocated to Srb, what happened was that in the development of the situation, the army was relocated from the territory of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina to the direction of Republika Srpska. What were the reasons for this decision, and who made this decision to withdraw the units, the Otric, Srb, Donji Lapac, Bosanski Petrovac, and so on, towards Banja Luka. Who made this decision and when?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision, I don't know who made it, but the real situation was the way it was. All of the people were in this small area, and the army was there. It was a conglomerate of some 50.000, 60.000 people in a very small area, and this had to be unplugged. They were expecting this to be done. The people had nothing to eat. They didn't take anything with them. They had no shelter. On that morning, on the 6th, to go slowly, because of the situation on the northern front, in Banija and Kordun, I was transferred. General Mladic sent a helicopter to get me, and urgently he transferred me. He told me to go there because that is where the column would be cut off, in Dvor, and there would be bloodshed among the people, and that together with his forces, I was supposed to prevent that. And those forces that were being pulled out were supposed to be engaged to security the flank to save the people. I left that area, but the headquarters and the president remained there. Probably it was not possible to stay in that area, technically, practically, any longer, because the pressure from the back was considerable. And we were expecting that the forward push of the Croatian forces would occur and they would find a lot of people in this area, and the roads would be very narrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And when this withdrawal did take place, did the army withdraw in an organised manner or was this just a spontaneous operation?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to Srb, it was organised. After Srb, everybody took their own families. Some put them on tanks. Everybody joined their own families, and there was no longer an army there, just an armed collection of people who were angry and unprepared for battle in that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And there was a lot of military equipment there; tanks, personnel carriers, armoured vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. People were using everything, even agricultural machinery, for transport. You can imagine how that was. It was a whole mish-mash of people driving all kinds of things in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe there's some things left out of the interpretation, beginning at page 13, line 15. If the witness could be asked again what they were using for transport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The question, Mr. Mrksic, was: "And there was a lot of military equipment there; tanks, personnel carriers, armoured vehicles?" And then before you told us about the use of agricultural machinery for transport, could you tell us what you said before you referred to this agricultural machinery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We called them "frites [phoen]" I don't know what you call that. They're called moto-cultivators, that's what they're called, small cultivation machinery.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not exactly sure what the term is in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anyway, it's something that is widely used for cultivation of the land in Dalmatia. Those who did not have such equipment would go to their dad, who was a tank operator, and they would ride on the tanks, because the armed units, when they arrived to that area, they were happy to see their kids, to see that they were alive, and then they took them with them. This was normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: According to what you said just now, was there an inter-mingling between the soldiers and civilian population, or, rather, military vehicles with civilian vehicles which were being used by the population? Was it all inter-mingled?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have an army and people; we had an armed people. These were our soldiers, peasants, producers. They would spend six hours on their positions and twelve hours at home. We didn't have a professional army so that we could separate an army who could go to this front or that front. The people were living normally there, where they were. These were all armed populations, and of course it was all intermingled. There were trailer trucks, buses there. I don't have to mention all of them. All kinds of means of transportation that could be found in one area. The whole town had to be moved. There were private vehicles there, many of them there. Whoever got their hands on whatever was what they used for transportation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, may I seek one clarification. You explained to us that even civilians would be transported on tanks, civilians being transported on military vehicles and military means of transportation. Was it also the other way around, that soldiers would be on civilian means of transportation, like tractors, like whatever was available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everybody took their own tractor, and when they saw the family, if they didn't have to operate or drive a military vehicle, of course they would take over the driving of the tractor from their wife or their son. This is in the depth, when we crossed over into Republika Srpska, then it was totally intermingled. As far as I'm concerned, it was no longer an army; it was a population. As soon as they crossed over to Republika Srpska, at the first check-point, they laid down their arms or their weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: According to a recollection, Mr. Mrksic, what was the date when the last military units left the Republic of the Serbian Krajina and crossed into Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, we did have some units which were -- which were left behind in the area which was surrounded and which was secretly trying to get through without combat, so there were groups that were reaching the place after 15 days, 20 days, and reporting to Kosara, where the Main Staff was deployed, parts of the Main Staff. So it was not that everybody left at the same time and easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But the bulk -- and the command structure?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until the 10th, I was at the bridge on the Dvor. After the 10th, no one was crossing over anymore, and that is when Republika Srpska demolished the bridge at Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So let's say by the 10th of August, the bulk of the units of the Army of the Serbian Krajina and the command cadre left the area, but there was some groups left behind which took even a week or ten days to get out of that area?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were pulling out clandestinely in order to not engage in combat with the units. They were trying to find some gaps and places where they could break out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As a commander of the Army of Serbian Krajina, were you in contact with those groups who were left behind, who were still in the territory of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina in the encirclement?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that I did, personally. My intelligence staff received those people, spoke with them, gathered the data; not for us, but for further processes. But you know how that is. Fear was quite a considerable factor, so it's incredible to know what they told about their return, how they managed to pull through, and the places that they managed to get out of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: According to your recollection, how many soldiers were there in these groups that remained behind after the army withdrew from the territory of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot exactly tell you. In some groups, there were five or six. They were breaking down into smaller groups deliberately, because a large group can be discovered quickly and then fighting can occur. They are searched for. So they kept splitting up into smaller groups. Later, even I heard there were some who had stayed behind for two years, they didn't dare appear, and they were found someplace in Petrova Gora. They were just like the Japanese who didn't know that the war was over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was there any combat contact of those remaining groups with members of the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not boast of fighting. I didn't hear of any fighting from them. Perhaps some did, but perhaps this person who -- or perhaps those who did engage in fighting were killed. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you say if those groups that remained behind were part of the military command hierarchy of the Army of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina or were they left to their own devices?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, being left to their own devices, well, they had their own zone, and it depends what was the position imposed on them in that zone by the enemy; were they cut off, were they in the encirclement. There were some cases -- the breakthrough from the Mount Velebit was like that. Of course, then it's normal that they would have to resolve their own problems by themselves. They would be cut off, cut communications with the command. If this happens, then they would pick among themselves somebody who would be in charge and lead them out. This is the usual procedure. This is the local population also. They knew the local area well. They knew where they could pass and where they couldn't, and so on. We didn't accept -- there was some partisan ideas in the beginning to apply some patterns as used in World War II. This is something that we did not wish to use. We didn't want to sacrifice the people. This policy is not something that was implemented in our policy, the policy of sabotage, to stay, to create problems, and so on and so forth. Anyway, you saw that for yourselves later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me what were the axes along which the members of those sections of the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina that were left behind were using to withdraw from the territory?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they didn't use the roads. They were moving through the woods. They were mostly attempting to cross the Una River and to reach Ostrelj, that area where the Republika Srpska was under [as interpreted] control. When they would notice their position, then the problem was would they believe them, that they were soldiers that had been left behind, or that they were not some infiltrators and that they would open fire on them. That was the most frequent consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This is the area of Lika and Mount Dinara that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the Lika and Dinara region. Well, you need to know that many did not manage to even come down the Mount Dinara. They stayed up there, and then they were crossing into Drvar as they knew best how.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, can you please tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please look at page 18, line 14, where I read the word "under." It makes sense only if one reads "in control."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That's correctly understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mrksic, you testified last week that there was an initiative that came from Mr. Martic to form the Liberation Army of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And we saw documents about that?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm referring here to D1522 and D416. D416, this initiative, was it implemented?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, its fate was as it was. It was not very realistic, and it was not really -- nothing was done about it. It just remained on paper. Of course, there was a ban on mobilising the population that had once been in combat and now had received the status of refugees. You could no longer get them to go back to fight. We could not reengage them, and this whole matter did not really move from theory into practice. I was respecting the decision of the supreme commander. We were aware that this would be something difficult to implement. It was just a way of proving that it was our desire to return to that area, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, allow me now to move to a different topic now, which was also touched upon in your testimony, and that is the so-called Operation Sword. Do you remember talking about it?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, please, in just a few sentences, what were the reasons to initiate this operation? Who and how -- who conceived the operation, and how was it supposed to be conducted?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operation was implemented by me. The idea was to use these free forces that I had formed, that I had at Slunj, to create conditions for Fikret Abdic, because he was receiving information from the 5th Corps, from people from that area, that they wanted to cross over to him. I was interested that as many people as possible supported Fikret Abdic, because he was protecting my back. This also happened in World War II. In these brief Ustasha offences from Kupa to Petrova Gora, the people would go to him, because there were units there who were helping our people. We were helping them, also, and we were helping them in 1994, when they were expelled. And I believe that this would be a way to resolve the vulnerable points -- the vulnerable point at my back, because I believed that Banija and Kordun could not survive without Fikret Abdic, in the same way that happened in World War II. This was not something that was conceived now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you. Let us set a time on this. When did Operation Sword commence?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I need to have a look at a document. It was in the month of July. The 30th of June, or the 28th, there was an inspection of forces, a parade, and then it took me some time to plan this, to put together forces. It may -- I think it was on the 15th, and it may have taken us seven to eight days, because we had threats from Livanjsko Polje and Grahovsko Polje. I had already started deploying forces to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In other words, in mid-July it was that the operation commenced and went on until the fall of Grahovo?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- they continued the operation with their own forces. I had pulled out my forces just ahead of the fall of Grahovo. I left earlier on, but I deployed elements of the Special Units Corps in that area. However, I saw that we were on a slope and they were up on top of the elevation, they could fire at us at will, and I saw that this was a battle lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In this operation, your enemy, let's call it that, was the 5th Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They would always link up with the forces of the Croatian forces, as they did in this particular case. They were the enemy to Fikret Abdic's forces. They fought him. I didn't even see them. I only assisted him by exerting pressure, and the idea was for them to see the extent and the strength of the forces they were faced with. And the idea was, of course, to allow these people to join Fikret Abdic's ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, tell us, what were the sort of military equipment and how were that you planned to use in this operation?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two groups of brigades of Fikret Abdic's who were supposed to engage the forces of the 5th Corps frontally. That would have been the thrust of the battle, whereas we would have provided artillery support. That was no secret. My special unit was two kilometres into the area, captured a certain elevation feature overlooking the area, giving us a good vantage point, but we didn't want to go into inhabited areas and we didn't want to be in touch with the population there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I now ask the Registrar to call up 65 ter document 3D00126. I have a hard copy for the witness, which may make it easier for him to follow the document through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, this is a brief or report made on the 26th of July by the Security Department of the Main Staff of the Serbian Army of Krajina, compiled by your assistant for security, Lieutenant-Colonel Rade Raseta. By looking at page 1, we can see that Operation Sword was supposed to commence on the 15th of July, in the early morning hours, as per plan. Are you following me, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 3 of page 1, this is what the report from your assistant for security states: "As part of the operation and its preparations, the SVK commander decided to use biological agents to poison consumer goods (flour, sugar, oil, dishwashing detergents) and to sell them by illegal trade to the 5th Corps, thus causing mass illness on the part of fighters and cause them to be 'au comba [phoen]' as a result." What is your comment on this report compiled by your assistant for security, Colonel Rade Raseta?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rade Raseta implemented the instructions of his superiors. You can see that the activity here was on several channels, and they were supposed to compromise the other side. I told my intelligence officer that we need to collect information because I wanted to put a stop to marketeering. Their answer was that they wouldn't be able to collect any information because there was no marketeering. I wanted to make sure that marketeering was no longer engaged in, so we had to device a ploy. We had people at check-points, making sure that none of these goods would go past. So what they devised was the state secret of trying to poison members of the 5th Corps, to cause them to end up with diarrhoea, so that they could no longer man their positions. And this was the sort of documents they bandied about in front of my family. This was done to compromise me and so that tomorrow they would have a lever to blackmail me. This was, on their part, a pure trade-off, and they wanted to get hold of certain information. You can see that there's a conflict of three services here, the Security Service, Intelligence, and State Security. That's what caused us major problems. I don't know what sort of problems you had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This particular report explicitly states that you decided to use biological agents and the method of poisoning?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no sort of poisoning. This was merely a cover. I had never heard of anyone poisoning anyone else. It was for the fighters, who were manning check-points, who, acting upon my orders, would not allow trucks carrying illicit goods to pass through, that they would, upon seeing this document, say -- not allow them to pass through.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Mikulicic please repeat his question. It's impossible to follow at this rate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you're invited to repeat your question. And I add to that that I invite you to make the necessary pauses between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will do my best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was: The allegations made in this report, that you decided about the use of poisoning agents and that you issued orders to that effect, is not true, therefore?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. That was a pure trade-off, and that was the subject of intelligence work, which was constantly operating. They were supposed to compromise me, and I am carrying this mark from Krajina to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This report also states that the normal dosage was used on an a individual, Goran Marjanovic, who was an illegal deserter of the Ustasha army, by injecting the agent into his liquid dish, unknown to the international humanitarian organs. In three days, he developed the above-mentioned symptoms that lasted for six days. He was given medical aid, which probably shortened the period of his reaction. Are you aware of this experiment?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is the first time I'm hearing of it and seeing this report at all. The problem was that security services produced reports behind their commander's backs, and this is also the problem that your army had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But this was your assistant?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's how my assistant operated. That was the system. I have the order which was a state secret, and I'm sure the Prosecutor has it. They, however, engaged in different sort of activities, and one should not trust whatever a security officer writes down. If we talk about this openly, about the work of security officers, let me go back to Vukovar, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, are you familiar with Lieutenant-Colonel Milan Krkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that he worked for the Intelligence Service. I think I saw him once or twice, if that's the intelligence officer we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was from Nis and that he was in the area of Topusko for a while, but that was not in 1995. I didn't see him there at the time. I saw Colonel Zimonja, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let's make this quite clear. We're talking about the Republic of Serbian Krajina, are we not?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Colonel Nikola Zimonja. I believe you're related to him.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's my extended family on my maternal side. I don't know which to degree. We're not close relatives, because had we been close relatives, he would not have provided President Milosevic with the sort of information about me he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know Colonel Mihajlo Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's the chief of the Intelligence Service. He was my subordinate, whereas Zimonja was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know an individual called Nenad Nisevic. He was a private businessman from Glina.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now that we still have the document on our screens --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can we turn to page 2? The document goes on to say that trailer trucks, loaded with goods intended for illicit trade with the 5th Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, were sent on their journey, unloaded their goods, and on their way back encountered certain unplesantries on the border because a patrol of the Army of Serbian Krajina confronted them. Nevertheless, they reached their destination in Glina, and I'm referring to the penultimate paragraph, where Nisevic, whom I asked you about, together with Zimonja and Krkovic, came to see Rade Raseta at Plitvice, carrying a briefcase full of foreign currency that they scattered on the desk and started counting and distributing. On the following page, it says that the total value of the goods sold, which was smuggled to the BH Army, the 5th Corps, was 2.237.000 German marks and that the purchasing price was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the amount.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And then page -- the following page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we first try to clarify what the purchasing price was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: 50.000 Deutchemark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The text goes on to say: While separating the German marks in new denominations, Nisevic counted and set aside 37.000 German marks and came in -- and engaged in a spat with Lieutenant-Colonel Krkovic as to why he was doing that and issuing it in new denominations. Nisevic replied by saying that the boss had explicitly instructed him that these had to be new German mark notes. Krkovic reacted by saying the following, So what if he's a general? Let him find a place to change them. Give him a part of it in shillings. Nisevic responded that this is the way things had to be, and Colonel Zimonja immediately wrote the name of General Mrksic on a folded A-4 piece of paper and placed 37.000 German marks in it, and put the package into his brief-case, undertaking that he would hand it over to him. Mr. Mrksic, did you receive any sort of money out of this transaction?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this is the first time I'm seeing the information. Let me tell you the truth, how it was and why I was under a pressure. There was one reason to exert pressure on me, the humanitarian reason; that there were people starving there and that they needed to give them supplies. I said that -- I produced a document, a state secret, that this trip should be made in order to obtain money for the Intelligence Service so that they could collect data, rather than have a situation as in Operation Storm, where I didn't have communication with my corps. I wanted the money to be used to purchase cutting-edge communication devices. This is something that everybody did on all sides throughout the war. Had anyone given any money to me, I would not have gone to work on the vegetable market in "Djeram," as I had to, once I returned from this stint together with my family, why -- I would not have ended up doing transactions with peasants on the market had I engaged in something like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The document goes on to say that: "In the meantime, while the foreign currency was being counted, Lieutenant-Colonel Krkovic repeatedly raised the issue of us, participants in the action, that we would have to be rewarded with 3.000 to 4.000 German marks and that this was something that General Mrksic would approve of."

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, why didn't they come to me with this sort of report? I would have had them arrested, all of them. And all the information, including the information about Dimitrijevic, ended up in the archives of the Intelligence Service, and we never got to buying these devices, in the end, the communications devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, how is it that you know that the information was centre to Aca Dimitrijevic when the cover page doesn't state at all who the addressee was?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, who else? My chief of security would send information to his superior chief. He wouldn't send it to the chief of the Main Staff, he didn't send it to me. This is the sort of service-specific specialist information. It would always follow the different professional chains; the intelligence to the intelligence, along their chain, and the security organ to their superior security organs. They wouldn't be reporting to those others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Remind us, please, Mr. Mrksic, who Aca Dimitrijevic is.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of security of the Army of Yugoslavia at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And then it goes on here to say that out of that amount of foreign currency, about 400.000 marks would go into the treasury?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did. The security chief did inform me that this did go into the budget, and we were going to purchase Motorolas and some satellite telephones or communications, some new systems from that money. But this did not actually happen, because the money was given to Belgrade. I know that during the withdrawal, the intelligence guy with the money always was escorted by a policeman so that nobody would grab the money from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At the end of this page, Lieutenant-Colonel Raseta, your assistant for security, says this: "The conclusion is simple. This convoy, as many others before, had the final goal of individuals to obtain material gain, and there is no doubt that the SVK commander, General M. Mrksic, is involved in this."

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know the information that was going around in Belgrade, that I had brought 15 million. I was always approached by Belgrade businessmen because they wanted to enter into business with me, that I could invest my money in these ventures. But when I was released from house arrest, I had to work on a vegetable market.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Two objections, Mr. President; number one, under relevance grounds; secondly, that there has been no foundation established for the document. The witness testified he had never seen the document before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Mikulicic, the relevance issue came to the minds of all three Judges already a while ago, and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me -- as far as the second objection is concerned, you have an opportunity to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness already stated that he was planning and executing the Operation Sword, Operation Match, as it calls, and that he participate in this operation with his own military forces. The witness was a commander of the Main Staff of the Army of the Republika Srpska Krajina, and he's witnessing here before this Court for a couple of days, and I think it's very important for the Chamber to see what is the relevance and what is the true position of that witness in the period concerning in his testimony. So I think this document is both relevant and also reliable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you're invited to move on to your next subject. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Russo, would you prefer to start now or would you prefer to have an early break?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I have no preference one way or the other, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let's continue. Mr. Mrksic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Russo. Mr. Russo is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: General, I'd like to begin by asking you some questions to try to give the Trial Chamber the clearest possible picture of what military assets were inside the town of Knin when the artillery attack began on the 4th of August. So if you could please focus your answers on the situation as it existed on the 4th of August, that will move us along much quicker. You agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, the assets were needed in order to relocate the Main Staff. We needed the jeeps, the bus, the transport vehicles, and the communication equipment that was mobile. There were no combat systems in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let me first begin by going back to some of the testimony you gave during direct examination. You stated several times in your direct that Knin was undefended. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, and that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I would like you to please explain to the Trial Chamber what exactly it is you mean, that Knin was not defended.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean to say that Knin did not have its defence unit, it did not have a defence system, it did not have engineering facilities, shelter, mine positions, positions, and so on. It was a free town, just like Belgrade, where people were walking around every evening and promenading every day as if it wasn't at war.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: To be clear, General, on the 4th of August did you have any combat units stationed inside the town of Knin?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 4th of August, I think that the command of the Dalmatia Corps had also left Knin. The Main Staff, or actually a part of the Main Staff, was the only force left in Knin, a part of the MUP, the Ministry of the Internal Affairs, and what was the security of the president of the republic, and of course the staff units, a police platoon that was there that I had that was securing the command. All the other forces had left already by the 3rd. There were no other units in Knin. There was a base, base command, but these were all non-combat units.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. The commands that you just mentioned, a portion of the Main Staff, a portion of the MUP, the Ministry of Internal Affairs, and the security for the president of the republic, were these -- the individuals in these units, were they all in the command building in down-town Knin on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some were at the hotel which is close to the command building. Some officers were billeted there, that HQ that was on duty. Well, I didn't sleep in that building that night. I was in town. Part of the staff units were on the ground floor premises, because the operations room was below ground, and the rooms that they were, other than the guards and fire duty officers, were outside when that first strike occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to be --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I want to say is that the police was there with us, the MUP, on one floor of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I just want to be as clear as possible. We have your command building in down-town Knin. You've also now pointed out the hotel where several of the officers were billeted. Other than those two buildings --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't catch that last comment.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a men's hostel, a men's hostel or a hostel. It was not a proper hotel. It was more like a bed-and-breakfast.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Other than that hostel and your command building, was the ARSK, or the MUP, or any of the other military commands using any other buildings or facilities inside the town of Knin on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think not, unless there is a police station that I never went inside; probably it was requisitioned in town to work with the population, traffic police and so on. There was nothing else that was occupied. There were no anti-aircraft or tank units. They were all outside of Knin, where they had been up until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. I also wanted to clear up something about the location of the command for the 7th Krajina Corps, and I think you touched on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, perhaps I could ask one clarifying question. The term "undefended" has been used several times. Did I understand you well that there was no formal declaration of Knin as an undefended town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I was told, when I was actually putting pressure on them and when I began to get angry, and when the danger appeared that Knin could be attached from the back, from Grahovo, from Livanjsko Polje, they did not have such units. They were not preparing it. They said it was a free town and it would not be struck, and that is something that I did not really believe; the mayor of the town, and the structures, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not precisely an answer to my question. My question was whether there had ever been, which I have not heard until now, a formal declaration that Knin was an undefended town.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not ask. I didn't find the Official Gazette. I didn't insist that they show me where that is stated in the Official Gazette. But the policy was conducted, and this was the explanation provided, that it was the capital town, and if we are brought into the position that we have to fight for the capital, because, well, the front was far aware. We were only beginning to think -- I was only beginning to think -- think about what I can build up quickly. However, the citizens of Knin were not thinking of needing to defend Knin. Knin must not be attacked. There were no units inside, so why would it be attacked, why?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're thinking in military terms, where I'm rather referring to the legal connotation of "undefended town." Is there any dispute between the parties that there was no such formal declaration? There's no dispute about it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: General, during your direct examination, and for the benefit of the Court and counsel, this appears at transcript page 18879, lines 9 to 11, General, you were asked by Mr. Misetic about the location of the command of the 7th Krajina Corps, and you stated that the command was located in the Northern Barracks: "... until combat activities commenced. When they did, just as my command did, he got up, got down to the railway station, and perhaps toward Strmica."

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The war or the combat location.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: "... at the IKM there, because he was practically on the slopes of the Dinara with some elements of his army. That's where the IKM was, and the command post was up at the abandoned railway station. I don't know what it's called, the one above Knin." General, can you please clarify for us, whether on the 4th of August, was the commander of the 7th Krajina Corps was inside the town of Knin or was he elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander, General Kovacevic, was at the forward command post. The former commander - what was his name? - he was at the railway station, and that's where we found him that night. Martic and I found him when we were conducting the relocation of the command. Martic remained to spend the night there near the railway station, and the Kovacevic was on the slopes and conducting the fighting as much as he could, as -- for as long as he could. He was slowing down the movements towards Strmica and Krno [phoen], at the forward command post. He was in a very difficult position at the last slope. He personally informed me about the situation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And the railway station that you're referring to, this is a railway station, an old one, outside of Knin; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Above the town, all the way up. We were speaking about it yesterday or the other day, about where the positions were supposed to be set up for breakthroughs into the depth. From that position, you have a visual over the entire territory and to the other side of the Dinara, towards Grahovo, Strmica, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just in terms of context, Mr. President, I just wanted to draw the attention to page 18879, lines 3 to 7, because I'm still not sure if this is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the witness's answer was clear. If there's anything that Mr. Misetic wants to clear up on redirect, he's certainly free to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you give me just one second to read both portions. Mr. Russo, if I read and compare page 18879, compare it with page 35, line 21 and ongoing, I can't say that matters have become much clearer. It's, as a matter of fact, rather confusing, if you read it too. I would appreciate if you would take that step by step, by short questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I just want to be clear, it's not my intention to establish exactly where he was, but, more importantly, where he wasn't. So that's the point of my questioning. So I'm going to take it -- I'll take it from the beginning, and then we'll see where it goes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, fine. If that's your intention, no problem. Sometimes if you know where someone is, then you also know where he is not; that is, at any other place compared to where he was. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: General, let me ask you again. When the combat began on the 4th of August, was the command of the 7th Krajina Corps inside the town of Knin; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Objection to the form of the question. He's asked now two different questions. The first one was "Mr. Kovacevic," the second one was "the command."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's such a question which can be put to the witness. At the same time, at the same time, it's not following my invitation. Mr. Mrksic, Mr. Kovacevic, early morning hours, 4th of August, where was he, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacevic, on the 1st, the 2nd and the 3rd, was up at the Dinara slopes the whole time. He was at the forward command post, managing the company or two companies that he had managed to gather, the soldiers he had brought up from the forward positions, and he was there to prevent speedy movement. He was not at the command. The command left early, just like the IKM left early. They had gone to the railway station. I don't know if anyone was left behind in the barracks. Perhaps some of the logistics people or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you're telling us is that on the 1st, the 2nd and the 3rd, he was up at the Dinara slopes. My question was about the morning of the 4th. Where was he then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was at the same place where he was on the 3rd; on the slopes, in battle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you were asked about General Kovacevic earlier today, and then you moved to the former commander who you said was found at the railway station. So that was not Mr. Kovacevic who was found at the railway station; is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just like the command of the Main Staff divided into the part that went to the forward command post, the corps command also divided, and a part of the corps command went up to this wartime command post during the day. You know that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the person found at the railway station by you and Mr. Martic was not Mr. Kovacevic. Did Mr. Kovacevic leave his position at the Dinara slopes? And if so, when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would really need to read his report, the one that he submitted, as to exactly when he left, but he probably left during the night because -- the following day and during the course of the day before the forces entered Knin. I mean, I really cannot know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say he probably left during the night, you mean the night from the 4th to the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That night between the 4th and the 5th of August, the Main Staff also left Knin, so I expect that probably --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In your answer, you are referring to during the night. I just want to know from you which night you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The night between the 4th and the 5th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, do you know -- apparently you're not sure that he left at that time. Did you know where he went when he left that position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When he left the forward command post, he was moving with the forces. It depends on the pace of the attack by the enemy. But up at the command post at the railway station, we found an ordered command post with beds, officers inside. I entered, received the reports about the situation. I issued additional instructions to stabilise the defence at the elevations above Knin, and I then left President Martic. He said, I cannot go on anymore. Beds are here. I'm going to stay here with the commander and my security. And he spent the night there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said he was moving with the forces. Do I understand you well that he did not return to Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not to Knin. From Strmica, he went right away to the place where his brigades were pulled up from Dalmatia, and he went up to the command post, and then later he came to Srb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said he went right away to the place where his brigades were pulled up from Dalmatia. Could you be more precise on where that approximately was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be closing the road leading from Dalmatia to Srb, above Knin. So gradually it was actually the -- done to secure the pullout, the withdrawal. And that's where the railway station is, more or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you say that's where the railway station is. Which railway station exactly do you have in mind now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it was an abandoned railway station that used to operate. Before, at the time it was disused, it was above Knin, at a ridge near the asphalt road leading to Srb. It was out of town completely. It has its name. I don't have a map here to be able to tell you what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any dispute about the parties -- about what railway station Mr. Mrksic is talking about? What distance from the town of Knin, Mr. Mrksic? What distance, approximately, from the town of Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you take the winding road up there, it's perhaps another three or four kilometres along the road, along the right side, where the railway tracks lie. There is a road up to that station. Perhaps Misetic knows what the name is. I don't know. I was only there for a brief period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, of course, I'm not inviting for you to give any evidence, but if, as you may have noticed --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When I testify as an expert later, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In what case, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll do the Theunens rebuttal. Just kidding. You asked whether it was in dispute. I so believe it's in dispute. I think the location of the forward command post is going to be in dispute, vis-a-vis this witness. Moreover, there's a bigger issue, Mr. President, which is: It's my understanding that the Prosecution -- based on an e-mail that I received from Mr. Russo last night, they're going to argue that the location is someplace, which I won't mention in front of the witness, which for months, at the beginning of this trial, they took a different position that the place where this IKM was located was actually being shelled by the HV and was a non-militarised place. So it's quite a complicated discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you during the next break -- Mr. Russo, is there any way to provide a map so that the witness could assist us, because you want to know where Mr. Novakovic was not. As I said before, sometimes it helps if you know where he was. Any way to provide the witness with a map later so we could look at it as well? Railways are usually --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Two points, Mr. President. The first, looking at the transcript, at line 22, you said "Mr. Novakovic." I believe it's Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I misspoke. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Second point, Mr. President: I don't necessarily want to -- I mean, I understand that the witness perhaps doesn't recall the name of the place. However, my only purpose was to establish that it was not inside the town of Knin. I believe the witness has already testified to its location. I don't believe I actually possess a map which indicates location of an older railway station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that's what you want to establish, then that is certainly what the witness told us. He told us about a winding road and three to four kilometres out of town. Now, I have -- before we have a break --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, again, I apologise for this, but I'm going to have to object to Mr. Russo being allowed to state where it's not. As I said yesterday, they want to eat their cake and have it too. The place where they think it is, but don't want to say, is also part of their case in-chief against us. And they should be compelled to now state that the location is where we spent months in this trial fighting about whether that place had military positions in it or not. And as a matter of procedure, they shouldn't be allowed to say, Well, we don't want to say where it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, if there is a dispute about what that position is, so I think it would be -- it would assist the Chamber in knowing what is on your mind, in relation to this, and also to know what Mr. Misetic's position is. Even if you would not ask the witness, at least the Chamber would be better informed as to what the dispute exactly is about, if only by location. Yes? Is there any way that you could sit together with Mr. Misetic during the break and to see whether you say, This is where --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, first of all, I don't have any problems stating our position. I don't know how much evidential value it will be for the Trial Chamber, but let me just try to clear up with the witness this particular location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I had one question remaining. I have to find it again. Could you tell us where he then went when he left that position, and when that was, this, I understand, deserted railway station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you mean General Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I should have been clear. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He left that position -- or, rather, he wasn't there when I got to that place. His command was there. He had not yet arrived, General Kovacevic. But President Martic, who subsequently arrived and spent the night there with his policemen, told me that they left in the course of the night, and that in the morning, when he awoke, they were no longer there. They wanted Martic to join them, but the policemen who were his escorts said that they should leave him sleep because he had not had a chance to sleep. It was on the 5th, in the evening, that Kovacevic got to Srb to report to me on the events and on the actions taken by the units. When he got down the slopes, Knin was empty. He got up to his command post and probably decided, together with his units, to change positions. He came to report that he had under his control the intersection that was vulnerable, the intersection from Gracac. He also reported that there were many people, the population who were there, and he didn't know what to do with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm trying to fully understand your testimony. You said: "He wasn't there when I got to that place." And we're talking about General Kovacevic. You said --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said after that: "Mr. Martic arrived and spent the night there."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And he apparently told you that they left in the course of the night. Who are "they"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you said he arrived after Mr. Martic had arrived, and that General Kovacevic left again that same night; is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your understanding is correct. It was that morning, probably before dawn, that Martic woke and found that they were not there. And apparently Kovacevic had invited Martic to join, but his escort would not allow him to wake him up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So Kovacevic had arrived after Martic had arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Kovacevic wanted Martic to join him, which did not happen, and the next morning, when Martic woke up, Kovacevic had gone already?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. Kovacevic -- or, rather, the president complained to me about being abandoned by my soldiers. However, they did ask him to join, but it was his policemen who played a role there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're not talking on why, but at this moment just to establish what had happened. We will have a break, and the parties are invited to report to the Chamber to what extent they can assist, perhaps even not in the presence of the witness after the break, what railway station is apparently in dispute, and we'll resume at quarter past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have the parties reached an agreement on what they disagree on?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I think we've at least agreed on that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It is the position of the Gotovina Defence that the witness, in talking about the location of Mr. Kovacevic before Operation Storm, most likely refers to Exhibit D159, about the fact that there was a Tactical Group 2 command post in the area of the village of Strmica on 31 July 1995. So now our position is the Tactical Group 2 command post is not the same as the forward command post of the 7th Knin Corps. Nevertheless, it's clear from the document that on that date, General Kovacevic was present there. However, we say that that is because General Mrksic has already testified to the fact that the 7th Knin Corps engaged in -- or attempted to engage in an offensive operation to take back territory near Grahovo in the succeeding one or two days. With respect to the railway station, the witness is most likely referring to the railway station at Padjene Stara Straza, which the Chamber has received some information about, and I will attempt -- I believe there's -- an exhibit was created specifying the exact location of that railway station earlier on in this trial.
