It is our position that General Kovacevic went to that location after the first day of Operation Storm, after the decision to withdraw from the city, and that that, in all likelihood, was the rear command post of the 7th Knin Corps. And it's our position, based on Exhibit D1516, paragraphs 6 and 7, which is Mr. Kovacevic's own report, where he says, and I quote -- he talks about the events on the night of 4/5 August. He says: "After the relocation of the command post of the 7th Corps Command and the General Staff from Knin ..." And then goes on. I believe it's -- I shouldn't say -- it's our position that that relocation from Knin was to the location Stara Straza Padjene, at the railway station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's about command posts and positions, and then persons are still left to be considered, who was at what --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, and that was going to be my final point, Your Honour. The position of the Gotovina Defence is the physical location of Mr. Kovacevic at any particular time, while it has some probative value as to the nature of a particular target, does not change, in and of itself, the definition of, for example, the Northern Barracks and its use and how it would be classified under the protocol. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we have two issues; where command posts were established and who was where at what time, and what consequences this would have for -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I will deal with it, I suppose, in redirect, but I think, just to mention for the record, I don't believe there's any evidence, for example, that Mr. Kovacevic sent a letter to General Gotovina saying -- I'm being facetious here, but, Forward my mail to my new address, which is now not at the Northern Barracks, but is wherever they say he is, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have never seen a change of address during such war situations. But anyhow, Mr. Misetic, it's -- Mr. Russo, positions are --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I'm not -- I'm not sure exactly what it is the Court is expecting. I certainly don't think it's appropriate for us to be arguing our case at this point. But let me just indicate, I'm not necessarily taking issue with some of the things that Mr. Misetic said. My only point in examination was, of course, to establish who is and who is not in the Northern Barracks on the 4th of August. The value of that can certainly be argued at a later point. I did want to take it, however -- and the reason I went in to Mr. Kovacevic first was because Mr. Misetic's questions, while directed at the command, the witness injected into his answers specific discussion about Mr. Kovacevic himself, so I was going to take it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that's at least one of the things that's perfectly clear now, that if we're talking about commands, not every commander is always at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That apparently is the issue, and that's clear. May the witness be brought into the courtroom again. And it may be clear to the parties to take the witness in whatever you want to elicit from him as evidence, to take him step by step, You're talking about a night. What night are you referring to? You're talking about a day. Who are you referring to? Because otherwise we easily get lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I have attempted to direct the witness, at the beginning of my examination, to the 4th of August, but I continue to try to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Both parties are encouraged and invited to take care that the answers are clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, could I invite you to keep your answers short. Often, you do not only answer the question, but you also explain why things happened as they happened. If anyone is interested to know why something happened, they'll certainly ask you. Could I also ask you always to be very precise. I gave you a few examples. If you're talking about morning, let me know whether it was yesterday morning, this morning, or tomorrow morning you're talking about, so that we always have clear facts. And if you keep your answers short. Often, after one or two lines, you've answered the question already. Then just wait and see whether there's any follow-up question. Let me be clear. There's no need to explain to us everything that happened in this period of time. There are certain matters which are of great relevance for us or, of course, this Chamber has heard other evidence as well and other matters that are less relevant. You could leave it to the parties to draw your attention specifically to those points that they consider to be very relevant, and if the Chamber wants to know further details, as you may have noticed, we'll ask you for it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And I am also eager to finish as soon as possible because of the visit on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Everyone is aware of that, Mr. Mrksic, and we'll try to achieve that. Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: General, you will recall a discussion during your direct examination in which you were educating Mr. Misetic about how you divide the command of a corps prior to combat operations. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. I was not -- not dividing the corps command, but of the Main Staff. What are you exactly referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm referring to the discussion where you -- and for the benefit of the Chamber and counsel, this appears at page 18858, lines 18 to 25. You were explaining to Mr. Misetic that when an attack is anticipated, as a general matter, and I'm not now asking you about your staff or any other particular corps, but as a general matter, a command is divided into three separate units: the forward command area, the rear command area, and the main logistics; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Now I understand what you're saying. Yes, that's how the rules regulate the matter. A unit cannot be without a command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask for a clarification of the question. Three separate units: The forward command, the rear command, and the main --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Logistics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We find, on page 18858, the witness is referring to three structures: the reserve command post, where the commander would be; the reserve command post, where the Chief of Staff was; and the logistics post, where the chief of logistics is. That is what he referred to on page 18858, lines 19 and following, preceded by where an attack is anticipated, the command has to be divided into three structures. That's what we are talking about. Mr. Russo, your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, General, what I'd like to do is to establish for the Chamber, specifically with respect to the 7th Knin Corps, the location, if you know it, of each of those separate structures on the 4th of August. So let's start with the forward command. Do you know where that was located, where the 7th Knin Corps Forward Command was located ?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forward command post of the 7th Knin Corps was on the stretch of the road leading to Grahovo, some 500 metres away from the confrontation line, which shifted depending on the developments. It was beyond Golubic, in the village of Strmica, in the direction of Grahovo, where the forward line of defence of the Croatian forces was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the rear command post, was that located at this old railway station about which you've been speaking?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you where exactly the rear command post was. I know that the main command post was relocated to the railway station. Was it called Zega? I don't know. Have you established what the name was? It was at that railway station that the main command post was. And as for the corps level, I don't know about their command posts. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: So if I understand your answer correctly, you're unable to tell us, on the 4th of August, where the rear command post was initially located for the 7th Knin Corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have been in Golubic, where depots were and where supplies could be obtained. Elements could have stayed behind in the barracks on account of the vehicles and the assets there. I can't confirm this. What I'm giving you are the possible locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And now for the third element of the structure, the logistics element for the 7th Knin Corps, can you tell us, if you know, where that was on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the one you just asked me about. It could have been either in the valley of the River Zrmanja, where warehouses and depots were and supplies were obtained from, and elements of it could have remained in the barracks. At any rate, the command was divided into three parts. I'm not sure where they were. After all, they were an element of the rear structure. Milovanovic would be the one to be better placed to talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Okay. General, there was -- and if it's my fault, I apologise. There was some confusion. I was asking you, secondarily, about the rear command post. You gave an answer. And then I asked you about the logistics post, and then you told me that's what you just asked me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe there may be an interpretation issue, how it was initially interpreted, and hence the confusion between Mr. Russo and the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I suggest, in order to avoid confusion, that you restart this whole -- because otherwise correcting questions and then trying to find the correct answer is not, perhaps, the thing that would work perfectly. So, Mr. Russo, you're invited to start this part of the examination again.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, forget about the last few answers. Mr. Russo will reintroduce the matter, because there might have been a translation issue. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: General, we will take it from the top. The main forward command post of the 7th Knin Corps, on the 4th of August, tell us where it was.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was mobile, and it was located on the slopes of the Dinara, from the village of Strmica toward Grahovo, the forward command post that always follows the commander. You have several officers, communications devices, and security officers. That's the IKM. The KM was at the railway station. The rear post was in Golubic, or elements of it remained in the barracks. I can't vouch for that. It would be logical for it to have relocated to Golubic, where all the assets were and depots, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you may have included everything in that one answer, which I'm thankful for, but I just want to reiterate to be clear. We've now established where the forward command post was; on the slopes of the Dinara. You say the KM, which is the rear command post --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rest of the command, the main command post. The KM is the main command post, the operational post, at the railway station. The rear command post was in the Zrmanja Valley. Whether it was partly in Golubic or partly in the barracks, I can't tell you, because it had to draw closer to where depots were and supplies were. I didn't go into the technology of supplies and all the other details.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: When you say the rear command post, whether it was partly in Golubic or partly in the barracks, can you tell us which barracks specifically you are referring to there?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Northern Barracks, I believe, where the corps command used to be stationed before it left.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Mr. President, I believe from my perspective, the matter is clear, unless the Chamber has further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: General, your command centre, where you were on the 4th of August, was the main command building which is on the main road in down-town Knin; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And you were in that command centre for most of the day on the 4th of August; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not -- well, I was there until nighttime. It was after 10.00 p.m. that we set out, when rocket fire subsided. We proceeded to relocate. I was there throughout the day, observing artillery fire. I was interested in that, because I had done something similar back in Vukovar, and I wanted to draw comparisons. That was when I found the spare time to do that, and I wondered at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to now move to asking you some questions about the shelling which you both observed and information that was reported to you. I'd like to take another look at an RSK intelligence report which Mr. Misetic showed you during your examination and ask you a few follow-up questions. Mr. Registrar, if we could please have Exhibit D389? General, you will recall that this is an intelligence report from one of your own officers, and it indicates some areas in Knin which had been shelled by approximately 10.00 a.m. in the morning on the 4th of August. Now, I'd like to focus on paragraph 4, and it indicates that the first strike was on the building of the SVK General Staff, and that is -- as you've testified, that's the building where you were; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: It also indicates that fire was later directed at the military barracks, and I believe you've also testified that that refers to the Northern Barracks; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how we called it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: The next target identified was the TVIK factory, and I'd like to ask you a question about that. General, the TVIK factory, can you tell the Trial Chamber whether there was any military use being made of that factory?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. It produced nuts and bolts that were sold in the market of Serbia, Bosnia, et cetera. It was a well-known factory of nuts and bolts. We received all the military assets from installations in Serbia. We could have produced 120-millimetre mortar shells in Lika, but we didn't have the materials required.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And to be clear, you said you don't think so. General, if the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina had, in fact, made military use of it, that would have been an asset that you would have known about; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly. Just as I knew of the factory in Lika, I would have known about this one as well, whether a nut or bolt was being produced for the purposes of vehicles or something of the sort, but I would have known if it had produced anything that would have had a bearing on the defence mounted by the Army of the RSK. I would have heard about it. General Bjelanovic, assistant for rear, would have informed me about it. It would have been discussed, despite the fact that I was there for only two or two and a half months and I had spent most of the time in Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The answer was simply, yes, you would have known about it. Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: The next target identified was the railway intersection, and I believe you've already testified that this was the main railway hub which was basically across the street and a bit further down from your command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And you've already testified that the ARSK was not using that main railway hub; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not using it. It may have been using it in 1991 or 1992 for an armoured train that they had, something of the sort, but during my time, it was not used and the railway was not operational.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. The report goes on to indicate residential buildings in the area beneath the Knin Fortress. Now, General, the area around your command building in down-town Knin is an area that's filled with civilian residences, apartment buildings, cafes and such; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Objection as for foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, is that an objection I seriously have to respond to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's hotly disputed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you'd ask the witness about everything we heard that could have been there, then we'll find out what -- whether it was filled or whether there were many, which is not exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just want to point out the fact I already have asked the witness about which buildings in Knin were being made use of by the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: General, were there civilian --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But that doesn't mean that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- I think you told us that down from the Knin Fortress, that there were government buildings there. That's looking down in the direction of the railway station. Could you tell us whether there were civilian residences there as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, they were all civilian buildings except for the one that President Martic built to be the headquarters of the president, with a few offices, an office for the reception of foreign guests, when we had talks with them, a secretary, and some rooms for the security. That was that one building. All the other buildings were civilian buildings. People lived there. I don't know if there were any cafes there. I didn't visit cafes. Perhaps there was some kindergartens there, too. But, anyway, that is what one could see looking out the window towards the fort. My office was towards -- it was facing the railway station, and I could see everything from UNPROFOR to the Northern Barracks. I could see the whole town from the third floor, and there were civilian inhabitants there. The civilian hospital was there. So it's not in dispute that there was firing on the town. I did mention the military facilities. All the others were civilian ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: General, you'll see, after it indicates firing on residential buildings in the area beneath the Knin Fortress, it says "Et cetera," afterwards, at the end of that list of areas being shelled. Could you tell the Trial Chamber whether you're aware, during the morning of the 4th of August, if there were other parts of Knin which were being shelled that are not specifically listed in this report?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, the entire Knin was being shelled except for the UNPROFOR base. In my estimate, I did make estimates because I knew how many divisions and batteries I had, without nine or ten batteries with multiple rocket-launchers, you could not cover it all. All the sectors were covered, and the firing system determined the intervals between the firing. So there was firing the whole time. These were systems that do not demolish buildings in the same manner that other systems do, but the noise created a major disruption, disturbance, for the citizens who were in these cellars. As I was observing, I was afraid that they would enter the office. It's about 30 minutes --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter kindly asks Mr. Mrksic to repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was firing as a system. The system is used for human targets outside, resting, lying about, to cover a large surface. And if you wish to take or capture a town, or if you wish to fight against those who are defending a town, then you would use artillery systems with shaped charges. There was no such destruction there. This was firing that had a psychological effect on me. As a professional, I was wondering why, why is this being done, who are they hitting when they have no positions. It was acceptable to me when they hit the command, the Presidency building and the barracks. That was to be expected, because military targets are expected to be there, but it was so precise that I really couldn't believe that the Croatian forces had such capabilities. These could only have been NATO capabilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, you earlier said that you were afraid that they would enter the office, and then you continued. You said it's about 30 minutes -- and then the interpreters couldn't catch your words. What was about 30 minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, shells were not falling; rockets were falling. This is a major difference, rockets from multiple rocket-launchers of 107 millimetres, NATO calibre, or 127, our Russian calibre, the former SFRY or the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just want you to repeat what you said when you started your sentence by saying, It's about 30 minutes. What was about 30 minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was my estimate. If each barrel, each barrel of the multi-barrel rocket-launcher, was charged and fired one rocket every 30 minutes, and there had to be 10 batteries, a battery would contain four weapons, times 18 -- or 12 barrels, and then you can calculate the number of barrels, and then you would have 800 to 1.000 rockets hitting Knin every hour. This is why they were all divided. Each battery had its own section of several hectares, six or eight hectares. Well, I'm just looking at it as a professional.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No problem with that, but I just asked you to repeat the line starting with: "It is about 30 minutes ...," and you started explaining your answer again. What did you say, because the interpreters just didn't hear you. You said: "It was about 30 minutes ...," and then just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I gave my own estimate, looking at the firing. If you had 10 batteries and you fired 30 minutes from each battery or each barrel, rather, because they fired at intervals, then you would almost have a thousand rockets hitting in one hour. Perhaps I don't believe it was that much. Perhaps at first impact it was that much, but later they were longer intervals, but the average was that you would have one barrel firing at 30-minute intervals. So in my estimate, you would have between 8.000 to 10.000 rockets falling in a 16-hour daily period of firing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear to me now. Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: General, you testified on direct examination about artillery located in Kninsko Polje. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was an artillery weapon called Nora of 152-millimetre calibre. It was the only one that had the range to reach Grahovo Polje. I think we only had two of those in the entire Knin Corps, compared to the Dalmatia Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And, specifically, you were asked about whether those artillery pieces were returning fire on Croatian positions on the 4th of August, and you stated, quote -- I'm sorry, for the benefit of counsel and the Court, this appears at transcript 18920 from lines 1 to 13. You stated, General: "I think that that artillery had already been pulled up there. As the units moved, as the people moved, it was pulled up towards Otric." Now, what I'd like you to clarify, General, is whether those artillery pieces were in Kninsko Polje on the morning of the 4th of August.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The weapons, there was nobody to operate them on the 4th up there, and they were probably withdrawn into the depth. I cannot know about those two weapons. All I'm saying is that I was present when the artillery guy was guiding the Howitzer fire, and that was creating large problems in Grahovsko Polje. This was two or three days before the 4th, before the attack. I was driving the supreme commander in a helicopter to the positions to see where his troops were holding the ridge, and we were watching how this small captain was guiding the fire at those forces that were preparing to open an attack against Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to be clear, General. Can you tell the Court how far from the town of Knin proper those artillery pieces were located?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those artillery pieces were practically beyond Crvena Zemlja, which is some five or six kilometres -- or four kilometres distance from Knin, that they would -- so that they would be able to reach Grahovsko Polje. When the aggression began, they had no targets practically in Grahovsko Polje. They had to pull out, and then the 120-millimetre mortars took over.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You've answered my question. Now, you've testified several times that you lost your communications capability sometime during the 4th of August. Now, the reason, General, that you lost communications from within Knin was because the repeater station at Celavac had been partly destroyed and taken over; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And after that repeater was taken out of operation, was it possible for you to communicate with your troops in the field?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our communications system relied on relay communications, which we considered to be protected, but I can see that they were easily recorded and transcripts were made. Radio links could not be maintained because of electronic jamming of some radio stations. We were unable -- not even Motorolas could function. There was general jamming.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: General, can you explain to the Trial Chamber what relay communications are?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Relay communications are traditional communications system. They have antennas, they have protected facilities underground, and these are nodes where communications intersect. It's a whole relay network of the former SFRY that was somewhere taken over. I don't know how these divisions occurred. So certain forces were using them. These nodes had direct links to Petrova Gora to Zeljeva, from Petrova Gora to Zrinska Gora, from Zrinska Gora would go to Poposte [phoen] to Belgrade, to Sarajevo, to Zagreb, depending on where they were directed. These were so-called directed, controlled signals. Usually, it's a telephone connection. It's not a radio station, but you can actually speak on the telephone, use it just like a regular telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. General, I'd like to show you an excerpt from a planning meeting between President Tudjman and his top military advisers on the 31st of July, and then ask you a few questions relating to it. If we could please have Exhibit P461, and if we could move to page 25 in the English and page 47 in the B/C/S. And I'd like to begin with the comments of Mladen Markac. You will see, General, that Mladen Markac states: "Mr. President, as soon as we take Celavac as a communications centre and to all practical purposes the nerve centre of that part, their communications system will be finished and there will be total chaos." Then Zvonimir Cervenko intercedes: "Mr. President, I would like to ask, Domazet, please explain to me how these communications centres will go, in what order, in which phases?" Domazet replies: "In the first strike, which would be the onset of the operation, we head out to the command post of the 18th Brigade in Bunic which creates conditions ... for their system and enables the forces - Ljubovo is reached and placed under supervision. "Second, Celavac is in that same strike. We're going to Celavac for the purpose of leaving him only a part of the communication between Knin and through Petrova Gora, to listen in on to them. We shall do that by aircraft." And then someone interjects: "You mean from Plomina when you say Knin?" And if we could turn the page in B/C/S. Cervenko continues: "From Plomina to Pljesevica, and we have it so we can listen in to operative strategic communications. And the destruction of Celavac, we will take down all operative and tactical communications in the area of the 7th and 15th Corps. After that, when the operation in the northern part is launched, we shall go to Petrova Gora. We likewise leave Zrinska Gora so that we will be listening in to only one part of their communications, and finally it ends with Zrinska Gora."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, did you intend to say that Domazet continued, rather than Cervenko, because that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes. My apologies, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: General, were you aware that the HV were planning to leave your communications in some areas open in order to be able to listen in on operative and strategic communications?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. I was not left with that assessment, because we thought if they strike, they will strike and destroy all communications. This is new to me. I knew that we were expecting them to strike at the communications. That was logical. But we didn't know that they would use these espionage things to listen in to some of them and destroy some of them. We were not thinking about that at the time. Had they allowed me to have those connections, well, it wouldn't have mattered to me if they had listened in, but I was unable to talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I take it, then, General, that during the operation you did not become aware that your communications were being monitored; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right, I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. General, I would now like to talk about the military assets, which were in other towns, which were attacked by artillery on the 4th of August. And if you're able to assist us, please do so. If you don't have the information, that's fine as well. But I would like to begin first with Benkovac. Can you tell the Trial Chamber whether you had any combat troops stationed inside the town of Benkovac when the shelling began on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you that. But when I was touring the position, I saw that there was nobody in Benkovac, that there were no elements, elements of the combat disposition. All the elements were on the front-line or some line of defence. These are probably elevations, inclines, not towns. We were not including towns into the defence, as far as I know. But I didn't manage to tour the tactical level completely. I was dealing with major things; how to create a political and military situation so that we could move to negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Are you able to tell us whether there were any command posts or communication centres in Benkovac on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were barracks in Benkovac. I don't know if it was used for anything or not. I'm really unable to say right now. The corps commander or the brigade commander would have to tell you that, the Benkovac Brigade. I don't think that any attacks were carried out. The essence was that all inhabited places were attacked. Vrginmost was attacked and there was nothing there, and it was hit with all they had, and we were wondering, in Knin, where they got the equipment or the weapons from in order to be able to reach all the way to Vrginmost.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, General. If we could move now to Obrovac. Can you tell us whether you had any combat troops stationed inside the town of Obrovac when the shelling began on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the units were at positions in Obrovac before the combat began. The command of that brigade was there before. I don't know where it was relocated. I really don't know. It didn't stay in town, however, because Obrovac was relatively close to the forward end. So at the town itself, in the hole close to the sea, I don't think that there was anybody was left there. It was all up on high at Mount Velebit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And, likewise, are you able to tell the Trial Chamber whether there were any communication centres or command posts inside the town of Obrovac on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't say that right now. I'm afraid I would make a mistake if I said anything. I know that man. I went to see him a few times, I wanted to see what we could do up there at Velebit, but I didn't see anything that would significantly indicate to me that these were important positions. A brigade command with five, six officers, you can put that anywhere. They're easy to locate anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And the last town I'd like to ask you about is Gracac. Again, did you, as far as you know, have any combat troops stationed inside the town of Gracac when the shelling began on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gracac didn't have any forces, as far as I know. It was in the depth, and the brigade that was up there, that was going from the -- well, the Gracac Brigade was more forward, in the direction of Gospic. I don't know. I didn't hear of any military forces being there. I didn't ever have the opportunity to pass by there and somebody would say, Well, come let us see there is such and such a force there. Nobody ever took me there. I really don't know. Perhaps with the moving of the front, the forces arrived there. That is another matter altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, finally, were there any, as far as you know, command posts or communication centres in Gracac on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It should all have been up at the facilities up there, because Gracac is in a depression. I really cannot answer that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's fine, General. Thank you. Now, I'd like to discuss with you how the artillery attack was actually conducted, and you've already given us some testimony about that. In particular, you've stressed how precise you perceived the attack on your command building to be, and I'd like to show you another excerpt from the meeting with President Tudjman and his advisers. If we could move to page 15 in the English, page 28 in the B/C/S. We can move a bit further down in the B/C/S, please. Thank you. In this discussion, General, President Tudjman begins: "Is an attack on Knin possible without hitting the camp which UNCRO-UNPROFOR has there?" General Gotovina replies: "At this moment, we can engage in extremely precise operations at Knin, systematically, without aiming at the barracks in which UNCRO is located." In parentheses you see: "(We have all the photographs and know exactly.)" If we could turn the page, please, in B/C/S. Domazet interjects: "In those southern barracks, and his forces are to the north. Therefore, we can fire with great precision without it coming in the line of fire ... a little to the south of Knin, that has been precisely ..." Finally, General Gotovina says: "At this moment, all of our weapons are guided, directly guided." General, from what you observed of the artillery fire in Knin, did it appear to you that General Gotovina was, indeed, using guided weaponry on at least some of the areas shelled?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I need to say again, for me, as a professional, this was a new system, a new thing, to hit right from the start without destruction 100 per cent. Everything else that they were hitting with the multiple rocket-launcher was the way it usually happens, it was dispersed fire, but in this other case, they were making very precise strikes. I believe that they were probably using a GPS for this kind of precise guidance. This is not something that the Croats could have had. Possibly the French could have had something like that or someone else, just like it turned out to be in Sarajevo when the UNPROFOR forces were meting out punishment, where they would hit their target with the first shell. If this was Ante Gotovina who was doing that on first strike, then I really can say hats off to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, you testified earlier about the first strike in which a projectile landed in the car park of your command building, destroying several vehicles; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and a soldier was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And other than that strike, can you tell the Trial Chamber whether your command building received any other direct hits during the day on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did not receive a single hit, and I really wonder at that; if they were able to strike the first one, that they could have struck all the rest and entered the town and finished the business quite soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, General. In regard to the shelling of your command building, you testified, and this is at transcript page 18901, lines 5 to 10, and you state: "I found it very strange that the commander continued, the commander of the operation, to pound artillery with such precision artillery targets in town. And had he continued, we would not have been able to remain at that command post. That was strange. That was what I found strange. I did not really investigate it further, but at that moment, that's how I felt." Now, General, what you found so strange was the fact that your command building did not continue to receive such precise attention from artillery; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Rockets flew by, and some of them may have grazed the roof or something like that. We, and I mean officers and I, were not afraid of it. The civilians were. But the sound of it, its whizzing, the threat of it hitting the window and killing the individuals inside, was something that made civilians very afraid. I told you that I saw civilians, women and children, holding hands on their ears, frightened out of their wits. When I got into one of the cellars, they asked me about what was it that they were hitting us with.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: General, you did indicate, as you've just said, that you had taken shelter in some cellars. Was this in civilian residential buildings or was it an official building?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, all these were blocks of flats, civilian residences. As rockets started flying, I had to find shelter in any nearby buildings. So they would get me out of my car. And in several such shelters, cellars where I had to find refuge on my way to the command post, I always had the same sort of reaction on the part of the people there, the same sort of situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, at transcript page 18919, lines 5 to 7, you testified that the rockets which were used against Knin were Oganj rockets, 128-millimetre rockets. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and 107, I also said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: General, did you have information or were you aware of the HV possessing the Oganj weapons system?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially, these systems stayed behind in our barracks, and Eastern countries, which would sell such systems, would sell the exact same systems. Our intelligence services told us that several West-type multiple rocket-launchers of 107-millimetre calibre had been procured. I was interested in knowing what sort of formation, what sort of a system it was, that would have as many rockets at its disposal. Was it procured at a very cheap price? But whatever the case, under our military doctrine, such weapons systems are never used for inhabited areas and fortifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, in regards to the shelling in general, you testified, and this appears at 18925, lines 12 to 14, I believe: "I was only briefed that all settlements, all inhabited places in the municipality, all towns, were shelled. That was not logical. Rather than pounding the front, they were opening fire at villages where there were no combatants."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You started at line 21, Mr. Russo. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Apologies. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: General, do you recall saying that in your earlier testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, and I would repeat the same now. I found it strange, as an officer, a general, who had the experience of several battle-fields. I wasn't clear on what the objective was. Our assessments never anticipated that we would be intimidated and driven out. We had envisaged that if we had combat hand to hand, then we would be fighting, but part of the plan was not that we would be shelling towns, that we would be shelling Zagreb, or civilians. And we expected the same treatment from them. We expected that they would be striking the first or second positions, the command, artillery positions, whatever is customarily targeted by an army against an army, and not that they would be targeting the bridge at Vrginmost from 30 kilometres away. They hadn't even come out to their frontline of defence and they're already shelling the environs of a village, or they're striking Korenica while they're still -- their positions are still back at Gospic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: General, can you tell the Trial Chamber, if you know, what the reaction of the civilian population in these towns and villages that were shelled was?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They all wondered at what was going on, including those at Knin, and they asked the commanders what it was that they were after, because it wasn't expected that -- they weren't accustomed to villages being shelled. It was by sheer luck that I ordered corps commanders to practice the evacuation of the civilian population in the event of combat activities. However, this did not last for long. It was already by 9.00 or 10.00 a.m. on the 4th that I received reports on these strikes. We discussed these matters, and as well as the matters at Knin, and our conclusion was that they wanted to intimidate the civilian population and to shake up the first line of defence so that the fighters would abandon their positions and go home and see what was going on with their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, in fact, the citizens who were remaining in these towns that were being shelled began leaving those towns on their own in order to escape the shelling; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everyone tried to find refuge in relatives' places, because these were people who hailed from villages and knew the area and would try to find a place to stay with their relatives or in wooded areas. They wanted to evacuate children.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could please have Exhibit D923.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just have one matter to raise with the Chamber, outside the presence of the witness, before the break, whenever that's convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We started relatively late after the first break. If you would deal with the document, unless it would take very much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I may be on this document for a bit, Your Honour. I'll put myself in the Court's hands in terms of when the Court wants to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then perhaps "a bit" means more than two to three minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Possibly five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then perhaps it's better to -- how much time would you need, Mr. Misetic? Two minutes. Then please proceed, since it's on our screen now, and then we'll have a bit of a later break.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could go to page 6 in the English, and page 4 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: General, this is a document which you were shown by Mr. Misetic, and a few questions were asked of you. I want to focus on the part where it indicates: "In the area of Dalmatia municipalities, the citizens, on their own, individually or in smaller or larger groups, left villages and towns and moved towards Licka Kaldrma and Srb." That's a correct assessment, is it not, General, of what happened?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if we could move to the second page -- I'm sorry, to the next page in English, that's page 7, and remain on this page in B/C/S. And I'm interested where it indicates: "It is more than obvious that the evacuation would have taken place even if there had been no decision for it to be carried out." Is that your assessment as well, General, that the people would have moved out in any case in absence of the evacuation order issued by the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without the decision of the president -- do you mean the decision of the 4th, issued in Knin? Well, let me tell you, frankly, what the people would have done. The people are smarter than us leaders. They take decisions based on the way the situation develops. The people would definitely have seized every opportunity to find shelter; to the left, right, center, to forests, wherever. However, had the aggression from our backs not ensued, and had Knin not fallen, had the fighting taken place the way we anticipated, the situation would have been quite different. Then all the plans we envisaged, perhaps the Republic of Serbian Krajina would have fallen all the same, but the people would not have been driven out. Those who didn't want to stay would have moved out, and those who wanted to stay would have stayed. And most of the people would have stayed. Nobody left their cow, their piece of land and home, out of their own accord, on a whim.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Mr. President, this is probably a better time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, we'll have a break, but Mr. Misetic first wants to address a matter for which your presence is not required. So I'll ask you to be escorted out of the courtroom, and we'd like to see you back in anything between 20 and 25 minutes from now. Madam Usher --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope you will not speak badly of me, I hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I promise, I promise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, although now your subject matter is limited, could you please address the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to note for the record that, in terms of the Prosecution's case on the shelling, I'm confused about what the Prosecution's position is now with this witness. The whole Prosecution's case in-chief, including the testimony of their expert, Mr. Konings was that the HV used indiscriminate weapons in firing, and now the case that Mr. Russo put to the witness was citing to General Gotovina's comments on the Brioni transcript that, in fact, the HV had -- could have guided systems, and in essence, sought to confirm that with the witness. Now, if there's a change in theory, it's too late to do that now, as far as we're concerned. And if there is no change in theory, and if, in fact, Mr. Russo's position is that the type of weapons systems used were indiscriminate, that case needs to be put to this witness under Rule 90(H). Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, I'm going to object to these continual insistences that the Prosecution state a position on this or that. Our position is in our indictment, in our pre-trial brief, and will be finally summarised in the final trial brief. Let me just state, to end this particular issue, that Mr. Misetic is well aware of our position, and it is not in relation to any particular piece of artillery, but that it was an indiscriminate attack and also a direct attack on civilians, and that can be for many reasons; using guided weaponry to intentionally fire on one area or another, or using indiscriminate weaponry. In addition to that, our positions have been laid out quite plain. The witness has provided evidence, based on his experience, that he believes guided weaponry was used. There is other evidence in the record to suggest that his assessment is correct. If, in fact, that is the case and General Gotovina had guided weaponry at his disposal, that again raises the issue of why military objectives were not more precisely targeted, were not more damaged than they were at the end, which is consistent with the Prosecution's theory that the main military objectives in the town suffered little to no damage, despite either an ability to do it or an inability -- an unwillingness to actually make them targets so they could take them over; basically, to feign that they were firing at these targets, with the actual objective being to target the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is incorrect we've already cited in at least one filing to the Chamber the precedents set in other Chambers. The Prosecution, in the Defence case, cannot alter its theory. There has been no position taken by the Prosecution. In fact, I dare say the exact contrary position has been taken consistently by Mr. Russo and the Prosecution, and specifically with Mr. Leslie, Mr. Konings and several others, that the HV systems that were used were indiscriminate weapons, per se. And, in fact, Mr. Russo elicited testimony from Mr. Konings that what the HV should have done was lay siege to Knin and engage in essentially taking the city without using the weapons, if they didn't have them. The Prosecution is in a different position, now that we are in the Defence case. They cannot do what they were doing in their direct examination, which is, We'll ask questions, but never put our case to any specific witness, and we'll argue it at the end of trial. In cross-examination, they have an obligation, under 90(H), to put their case to the witness. If -- if the Prosecution now concedes that there was precision targeting of certain targets in Knin, but the Prosecution cannot explain or thinks there was some hidden weapons system that wasn't discussed with Mr. Rajcic, that wasn't discussed with Mr. Konings, that wasn't discussed with General Wesley, then either they have to come forward and provide a basis for that assertion or else there should be a stipulation that the weapons systems they put to Konings and Rajcic were, in fact, used in a manner that was precise. But now to play games with this witness to say we're going to eat around the edges, but never put to him, is improper under 90(H). And they have an obligation, now that they are on cross-examination, to put their case to our witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, our position has not changed. We're not indicating that the weapons systems which Konings testified about, which Mr. Rajcic testified about, we're not taking a different position to what those weapons systems were capable of. Nor are we changing our position with respect to the indiscriminate nature of multiple-barrel rocket-launchers for use in civilian-populated areas. The witness has given evidence that multiple-barrel rocket-launchers were used. He believes they are inappropriate. That is consistent with the Prosecution case. Rule 90(H) only requires us to put to him the evidence which is in contradiction of the evidence he has given. He's now given new evidence, which was not in the record before that he believes some kind of guided weaponry had been used. My point in exploring that is to establish that if that, indeed, if that is the case, should the Chamber find that, based on his testimony, that there is additional evidence to suggest that the use of that weaponry, whether it was, in fact, used or not, was used in a manner consistent with the way the Prosecution alleges the weaponry was used; in other words, used not to target civilian -- military structures, but rather the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, this is -- it's absolutely a new theory, and he used the Brioni transcript not just to say this is what the witness said on examination but then put a different case to using the Brioni transcript. And, again, I don't know the citation off the top of my head, but I believe in the response -- we filed a response in which we cited to the precedents in other Chambers that they cannot now -- this is our time to answer what they alleged in their case in-chief. To now tell us that they're going to now argue that, in fact, it may be that the Croatian artillery was so precise in the first barrage that now they concede that, in fact -- not just concede, but now positively put to this witness that General Gotovina said at Brioni that we can guide our artillery precisely, and, therefore, we're going to now use that argument as part of an indiscriminate campaign, is a new theory being raised in the Defence case. This is, again, our opportunity to raise what they argued in their case in-chief. That argument was never advanced in their case in-chief, and they shouldn't be allowed now to raise a new argument; in essence, to say the opposing general perceived it to be so precise that he thinks NATO was targeting him, to say, Well, yes, we, the Prosecution, now concede that, and we say that's proof of an indiscriminate campaign. At some point, their case in-chief has to stop and our response to that case has to begin. And, again, Mr. President, I would just state that the theory with Mr. Konings, the theory with Mr. Rajcic, was that the weapons systems used were, themselves, per se, indiscriminate. And that case was put to Mr. Wesley as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm not going to continue to argue the issue, other than to state that our position was not that these weapons were, per se, indiscriminate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask you to listen to Mr. Russo's argument in the 98 bis hearing. That's exactly what he said; in the context of this case, those weapons were indiscriminate.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That is correct, Judge, I said in the manner in which they were used, not that these are as the Defence has continued to point out, on some list of prohibited weaponry, such as cluster munitions or nuclear weapons. That's not the issue. The issue is the application of the weapons system in this particular town on this particular day, given the civilian and military situation in the town. Now, again, I will state our theory of the case has not changed. This is a new piece of evidence that the witness has provided to the Court, and I'm simply exploring the basis for his assessment. Our theory remains the same. We will not be arguing a different theory in the final trial brief than we put forward in the indictment or in the pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, just if I may respond to that. He just acknowledged that he argued it at 98 bis in the context of this case. Of course we're talking about the context of this case. Now he's suggesting, however, that what he said at 98 bis wasn't, in fact, true because there were precise targeting that was taking place in the context of this case, and that is a new fact. The argument in 98 bis was the HV was using indiscriminate weapons in the context of this case and that that, in and of itself, constituted an unlawful attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since you raised the matter, Mr. Russo is the last to add one or two lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Just to correct what Mr. Misetic just said, I have never said, nor should I have been required to state a position, but I did not say that there was precise targeting that was taking place in the context of this case. I didn't say that. The witness provided the evidence, and I explored it with him. That's all that's happened here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider the matter. To start with, we have 20 minutes to think about it, because that's how long the break will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, the Chamber has considered the matter raised by you. I've not explicitly given the Defence teams an opportunity either to join or not to join, but at least there was no request to further address the matter. Mr. Misetic, the Chamber has come to the conclusion that the answers the witness gave in relation to a number of, if I could say, high-precision hits in the early stages have not triggered the obligation we find in Rule 90(H)(i), that is, that if a witness was able to give evidence relevant for the case for the cross-examining party, that counsel shall put to that witness the nature of the case of the party for whom that counsel appears, which is in contradiction of the evidence given by the witness, it's the Chamber's conclusion that the content of the evidence has not triggered an obligation to do so. But the matter seems to be more complex, that it's whether or not answer an contradicts the Prosecution's case also depends on an understanding of what the Prosecution's case is. And we have clearly heard that you are saying you are shifting your case from one area to another. So despite this conclusion by the Chamber, if either you or any of the other Defence teams would like to further raise the issue of shifting the Prosecution's case from one point to another, that you are then invited to make written submissions on it, which, of course, could deal with what exactly your understanding at this moment the Prosecution's case is, whether it is shifting, and why, in your view, it is shifting, which of course then also might shed a different light on what contradicts the Prosecution's case and also what to do about it in this stage of the proceedings. You are then invited to make written submissions on the matter, and then the Prosecution will have a possibility to respond to that. But at this moment, as far as this witness is concerned, there's no need to put the case -- the Prosecution's case to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we will go ahead and do that. I do wish to state, however, that I was not raising the issue that the witness's evidence of high-precision hits is in contradiction with the Prosecution's case. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I refer to a portion of the evidence where he, and he said it several times, I think he mentioned GPS twice, he was talking about NATO-like, whether that is -- whether that was exclusively used and whether it's the Prosecution's case that it was not part of the weaponry that was used in the -- on the 4th of August, so as to that only other weaponry had been used, is a matter which, of course, could still be further explored for the witness if any party deems fit to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, that's precisely our position, is that the issue is the Prosecution now putting a case that the HV was using guided weapons. And if I could, in addition, state that essentially our position, Mr. President, is that this is the Defence case in-chief. We've been here 15 months in trial. We'd like to hear the Prosecution put this shelling case to somebody, and 15 months should have been sufficient time to actually put that case to someone, and we shouldn't have to be filing submissions to seek further clarifications from the Prosecution. You will recall that when Mr. Wesley testified, the Prosecution raised the same position with respect to the Defence having to put the case of targets to Mr. Wesley. The Chamber granted that request and we had to come back an extra day to do it. We would hope that at some point the Prosecution be required to pick a witness, and, similar to what we had to do with Mr. Wesley, that they have to do with some witness of the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. Could the witness be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: General, the evacuation which was ordered by the Supreme Defence Council, that evacuation was never intended, much less planned, as a permanent removal of the entire civilian population into Bosnia, was it?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That should not have been that. The population was supposed to be moved. We were always expecting the international community to stop that at any point and for us to return from Srb.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, your plan was to move the civilians to the area of Srb and to hold out until international pressure forced the Croatians to stop their advance; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if that had --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, because we didn't have the forces to stop them ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if that had happened, you foresaw that the people would have, in fact, returned to their homes and villages; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have been the option because of which I had come to be a commander in the Krajina. That would be the solution that President Milosevic and Tudjman agreed on. But the change of plan came from the Tudjman side, probably due to a historical desire to carry out these aspirations. I think this is a major mistake imposed on the Croatian people. President Milosevic told me, Mile, this is a chance. All our negative past that we had behind us for us now to resolve positively, because you cannot resolve the position of the Croats without the cooperation of Croatia and Serbia, without Croats and Serbs. I would not have been doing my duty had I not been told that. I would not have gone there otherwise to lose a battle. I had never been unsuccessful in any of my assignments, I was always successful, and I was so struck by that fate and by that lack of trust that I couldn't get used to it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is unable to keep up with Mr. Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, the interpreters say they just can't follow your speed of speech. If you could please start again where you said: "I was always successful, and I was so struck by that fate and by that lack of trust ..." What did you then further tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After that, I said that I had taken that personally in a very hard way, and after that I proposed, at a government meeting in Bijeljina after that, that I be placed before the Military Court, because I felt that I had made a mistake and that I had not carried out the assignment given to me by President Milosevic. And I felt that I, by doing what I did, but I didn't have enough time, that we would move to a solution by means of negotiation, not by means of warfare. I didn't manage to do that, but they behaved towards me as if I had failed. I couldn't go back. They had -- they wanted -- they stopped me from crossing the border. Then I returned. I was placed under house arrest, and I was under house arrest for two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: General, I do understand that you have a burden on your chest to relieve. However, I'm hopeful to finish my examination in the next 20 minutes to allow you to visit your family, so if we can just move along. My next question for you is regarding this issue of encirclement. Mr. Misetic asked you many questions about the danger of encirclement by Croatian forces. You testified that if your forces had been encircled -- and this appears at transcript 18840, lines 17 to 19. If your forces had been encircled, you foresaw the involvement of the international community to help avert a massacre or a retaliation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right, correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, in that case, had you been encircled, you believed that your fighters would have disarmed and returned to their homes normally and had their rights guaranteed by the international community; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believed that, and that was the plan we had worked out, and that is why I had these concepts that I had issued, that were issued to the 2nd Corps --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The 21st Corps, Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- If things were going to come to that, the Kordun Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: But the Croatian forces did not seem to want to completely encircle you. That was your assessment; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Let me repeat. Had they kept the exit out of Knin, the winding road that leads to the road towards the -- towards the main road, nobody would have been able to go out only with one-third of the ammunition that they had, but the amount of ammunition they had actually would have meant that nobody could have left the town, including none of the command. But for me, that is an objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: General, you were surprised, were you not, about the fact that the Croatian Army did not press their advance to capture and to enter Knin as quickly as they could have; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That is why I was receiving criticism, Why did you leave when nobody had yet entered Knin, why did the people leave? Well, the people left because they were afraid that they would find themselves trapped in a circle. Nobody could stand that firing anymore from the mortars and the rocket-launchers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And you testified that the HV could have walked into Knin whenever they wanted because the MUP forces, which were positioned at the Dinara, had abandoned their positions, so there was no one to stop the HV from coming into Knin; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That is correct, and General Kovacevic himself was not able to do that with such a small number of forces. He could have entered Knin right away. I don't know why they waited until 1430 hours the following day, when they actually did enter. They could have entered on the first day as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, General, you testified at page 18984, lines 21 to 23. You stated: "But you didn't just cut off. You pushed, you instilled fear in the people, you frightened the people, and people had to flee. You pushed and you pushed and you pushed." Now, General, what you're referring to there is the fact that General Gotovina's forces had used artillery to push the people out, correct, had left them a way open; is that right? Is that what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that's how it was, but I don't know whose idea it was. I mean, it was a crazy idea. The force from the front were advancing as our brigades were withdrawing, so what I'm wondering about here is that there was no specific order of who would be in command of specific places and villages.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is kindly asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if such an order existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Russo. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll need about a session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which means, Mr. Mrksic, don't worry, your family visit will be on Wednesday. We'll certainly be finished.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Following up just on this last point, General Mrksic, in terms of -- apparently I take it that Mr. Russo wants to suggest that the HV should have encircled you all and trapped you in, so let's put it to you. Why didn't you just surrender? I asked you this question before.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whoever surrendered without sustaining any losses? You should have inflicted losses on me in the battle-field in order for me to surrender. That's number one. Number two, I didn't go there to wage a war, but to broker peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So is it your testimony, General, that you were the commandant of the SVK, yet you failed to take measures to defend your territory?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. First of all, that mischaracterises the witness's testimony. Second of all, it's a leading question and he's on redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask for some leeway here, in light of the nature of the case, and since Mr. Russo doesn't want to put his case to the witness, I would like to put a case to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could, nevertheless, find different phrasing of question, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Mrksic, did you intend to defend the Republika Srpska Krajina from a Croatian offensive operation; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not in that way. I wanted to do it the way it was planned. It was a surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And in the way the Croatians conducted their operation was a surprise to you, coming from the JNA school; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and not because I didn't know what they could do; rather, because they captured or got territory through Republika Srpska, which is a political matter I don't want to go into. I was banned from defending Krajina from that direction, as if we had two different peoples we were dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's ask this question: If the HV could have just walked into Knin, which is what Mr. Russo wants to suggest, why, at 2000 hours, did you order the decisive defence of Knin?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. Again, I'm objecting to the way this examination is going. If he wants to establish that there was an order given, he should ask the witness or put something to the witness. Leading him in this fashion is assuming facts which the witness is not testifying to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, that's completely false. My direct examination talked about the meeting in the HQ at 2000 hours, the order for decisive defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was on the basis of the report or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The report and as well as his testimony about he wanted to defend [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's any dispute about it, I'd always prefer that you take him to that portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm at a -- I'll be ready tomorrow, Judge, but for the last 15 minutes I may not have transcript reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then take your time and do it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General, the question is: If the HV could just walk into Knin, why did you order the decisive defence of Knin at 2000 hours on 4 August?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At which facilities? Well, you know what the decision was, that Knin would be defended in the features above Knin, not because of Knin but because of the people who would be withdrawing towards Srb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If the HV could just walk into Knin, why did you order the continued defence of Knin through the issuance of the order for decisive defence?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could not as well have ordered them to leave in order to make room for the Croatian Army. It was a moral issue, and we know which forces were involved and what happened. It's on that basis that I said that they could have walked in, and not on the basis of who issued which orders, which commander would order for a place to be vacated in order for the Croatian Army to move in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, if it would assist you. It's page 18946, the report by General Kovacevic is introduced where the decisive defence, if that would were assist you, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that if I gave you time until tomorrow to find it, you, nevertheless, pursued the same matters still without sources, and that's not what Mr. Russo had on his mind and that's also not what I had on my mind at that moment. Please proceed. Either you wait until tomorrow or you take now this --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I was referring to transcript references, Mr. President, but I will call up Exhibit D1516, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to raise two matters with you, General Mrksic. First is your order for decisive defence; and second is your testimony in answer to Judge Orie's question about whether General Kovacevic -- well, I'll get to that in a minute, but whether General Kovacevic ever returned to Knin on the 4th of August. And if we could turn to paragraph 6 in this document, please. Now, the first question. At paragraph 6: "On 4 August --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have to apologise. I said something about a report by Kovacevic, but it's the Uzelac report, isn't it, D1516?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
